title: Tides: The Moon’s Pull on the Ocean
objective: After this level you can explain why most coasts get two high tides a day and what spring and neap tides are.
summary: The Moon’s gravity makes two bulges of ocean water. Earth spins through both each day; the Sun makes tides bigger or smaller.

cards.headline: The Moon moves oceans. Twice a day.
Two bulges, not one
cards.body: The Moon’s gravity pulls on Earth’s oceans, stretching them into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. As Earth spins, most coastlines pass through both bulges, getting two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

cards.headline: The Sun joins in
cards.body: The Sun pulls on the oceans too, more weakly. Around new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine into extra-high and extra-low tides: spring tides. Around the quarter Moons they pull at right angles and tides are gentler: neap tides.

cards.fact: Spring tides have nothing to do with spring.
cards.context: They happen twice a month, all year round. The name comes from water “springing” up higher.

cards.headline: Tides: explained
learned: The Moon’s gravity makes two ocean bulges
Most coasts get two high tides a day
Spring tides: Sun and Moon lined up
Neap tides: Sun and Moon at right angles

options.label: The Sun’s heat
options.rationale: Heat drives weather, not the tides.

questions.explanation: Tides come mainly from the Moon’s gravity, with a smaller pull from the Sun.

questions.prompt: Why do most coasts get two high tides a day, not one?

options.label: The Moon orbits Earth twice every single day
options.rationale: The Moon orbits once a month.

options.label: Earth spins through two tidal bulges each day
The Sun makes one high tide and the Moon the other
options.rationale: The two bulges both come from the Moon’s pull.

options.label: The ocean sloshes back after each tide
options.rationale: The pattern comes from two tidal bulges.

questions.explanation: There’s a bulge facing the Moon and another on Earth’s far side. Spinning through both gives two high tides a day.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: spring tides happen at new and full Moon. What do those two phases have in common?

options.label: The Moon is closest to Earth
options.rationale: Phase doesn’t depend on the Moon’s distance.

options.label: The Moon is half lit
options.rationale: That’s the quarter Moons, when neap tides happen.

options.label: The Moon is on the far side of the Sun
options.rationale: At new Moon it’s between Earth and the Sun.

options.label: The Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line

questions.explanation: At new Moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun; at full Moon, Earth is between them. Either way they line up, and their pulls add up.
